page_purposes.default: Use this page to compare LEAP results with ESTO history and the 9th Outlook on a shared set of energy-balance categories.
page_purposes.total_demand: Start here for a whole-system view of final demand, transformation, supply and the principal energy-balance totals.
page_purposes.buildings: Use Buildings to review residential and commercial energy demand, including fuel totals and changes that need to be traced back to model assumptions.
page_purposes.industry: Use Industry to review industrial energy demand by subsector and fuel, with particular attention to large changes and differences between sources.
page_purposes.transport: Use Transport to review road and non-road energy demand within the economy, including fuel switching and the effect of the detailed transport model on LEAP results. International aviation and marine bunkers are not included here; review them on Supply or on the separate International transport page.
page_purposes.international_transport: Use International transport to review international aviation and marine bunker fuel as a signed deduction from domestic supply.
page_purposes.others: Use Other demand to review agriculture, fishing, non-specified demand and aggregate-only demand that has not yet been replaced by detailed LEAP branches.
page_purposes.non_energy: Use Non-energy use to review fuels consumed as feedstocks or materials rather than as an energy source.
page_purposes.power: Use Power to review electricity and heat generation, fuel inputs and outputs. LEAP's power transformation modules do not measure power-sector own use or losses within the transformation process. These are represented separately, so the charts on this page let you analyse power-sector own use and losses alongside the transformation results.
page_purposes.refining: Use Refining to review refinery inputs, oil-product outputs and differences that may indicate a yield, capacity or balance issue.
page_purposes.other_transformation: Use Other transformation to review conversion processes and transfers that sit outside power and refining.
page_purposes.supply: Use Supply to review how production, trade and transformation outputs meet the model's fuel requirements.
page_purposes.emissions: Use Emissions to review the emissions implied by energy demand. Read the page note carefully where aggregate-only demand prevents a detailed sector split.
page_purposes.transport_leap_vs_ninth: This diagnostic page provides a focused LEAP-versus-9th view of transport detail. Use it alongside, not instead of, the main three-source Transport page.
page_purposes.datacentres_leap_vs_ninth: This diagnostic page provides a focused LEAP-versus-9th view of datacentre demand. Use it alongside the main Buildings page.

page_notes.industry: Note: Occasional mapping errors can make a chart show something unexpected. If you think you have found one, please let the dashboard developer know.

total_demand.title: What appears on the Energy balance overview
total_demand.copy: This is a bespoke summary page rather than another branch of the detail tree. It brings together reviewed whole-system identities so you can locate a large imbalance or demand change before opening the page that owns the underlying flows.

table.caption: Energy balance overview contents
rows: Supply
Production (01), imports (02), signed exports (03), and signed international transport (04-05), with total primary energy supply (07) where available
Stock changes remain outside the projection-comparable supply total.
Final demand
Total final consumption (12), split into the major demand pages and broad fuel groups
Demand sectors are selected on a non-overlapping frontier; do not add their parents and children again.
Transformation
The reviewed total transformation boundary excluding transfers
Negative inputs and positive outputs can cancel, so inspect the transformation pages for process detail.
TFEC
Not currently displayed
Flow 13 is temporarily disabled because non-energy use cannot yet be separated from aggregate LEAP Other demand.

total_demand.title: Know what each overview total includes
total_demand.copy: These are reviewed comparison views, not a sum of every chart elsewhere in the dashboard. Parent, child and generated rollup rows can coexist in the source surface, so the renderer selects one non-overlapping boundary for each total.

table.caption: Overview measures
rows: Supply
Production + imports + signed exports + signed international transport
Stock changes remain outside this projection-comparable total.
TFC
Energy and non-energy final consumption
Use it to test the overall demand boundary before opening sector pages.
Transformation
Total transformation excluding transfers
Inputs are normally negative and outputs positive; compare the boundary, not a simple gross sum.

supply.title: What appears on Supply
supply.copy: Supply is organised by the balance flows that add energy to, or remove energy from, the economy. The table shows each Common flow and fuel on this page beside the native categories mapped into it for the participating datasets.

table.caption: Supply page contents
rows: Core flows
Production (01), imports (02), exports (03), and international transport (04-05)
Exports and international transport are displayed as negative because they leave domestic supply.
Balancing flows
Stock changes (06) and statistical discrepancy (11) belong to the Supply family
They may be excluded from the current presentation; if shown, either sign can be meaningful.
Products
Primary fuels, petroleum products, gas, electricity, heat and other reported carriers
The exact fuel detail depends on the selected Common-category scope and source coverage.
How to use it
Start with supply composition, then open the material flow-product pair
A supply difference can come from quantity, sign convention, product grouping or source coverage.

supply.title: Read supply signs before comparing size
supply.copy: The dashboard applies explicit display sign rules. A surprising sign is a prompt to check the source or mapping convention; it should not be silently reversed during review.

table.caption: Supply sign guide
rows: Production
Positive
Adds domestic supply.
Imports
Positive
Adds supply from outside the economy.
Exports
Negative
Removes energy from domestic supply.
International transport
Negative
Marine and aviation bunkers are supplied domestically but excluded from domestic energy use.
Stock changes
Either
Positive is a stock draw; negative is a stock build.
Statistical discrepancy
Either
A balancing signal to investigate, not an ordinary supply source.

international_transport.title: What appears on International transport
international_transport.copy: International transport contains marine and aviation bunker fuel, kept outside domestic Transport and domestic demand totals. It is a focused view of rows that also remain on Supply and contribute to TPES. The table shows each Common flow and fuel beside the native categories mapped into it for the participating datasets.

table.caption: International transport page contents
rows: Flows
International marine bunkers (04) and international aviation bunkers (05)
These are international movements, not domestic navigation or aviation.
Products
Usually marine fuel oils, jet fuel and other reported bunker fuels
The dashboard retains whatever shared product grain the selected datasets can support.
Signs
Fuel supplied to bunkers is normally negative
The negative sign means removal from domestic supply, not negative physical activity.
Supply relationship
The same rows remain visible on Supply and are included in TPES
This page is a secondary review view, not another amount to add to Supply.

international_transport.title: Keep international bunkers outside domestic transport
international_transport.copy: International aviation and marine bunkers are shown as negative because they are removed from domestic supply. Review them separately from domestic Transport and alongside Supply; a positive bunker value is a sign-convention warning.

power.title: What appears on Power
power.copy: Power covers electricity and heat transformation, combining the plant boundaries needed to compare sources that organise producers and technologies differently. The table shows each Common flow and fuel on this page beside the native categories mapped into it for the participating datasets.

table.caption: Power page contents
rows: Flows
Electricity plants, CHP plants and heat plants under 09.01 and 09.02, plus related power-sector own use
The specific Power roots take ownership before the broader Other transformation root.
Input products
Coal, gas, oil, renewables, waste and other fuels used by plants
Transformation inputs are normally negative.
Output products
Electricity and heat
Outputs are normally positive and should be reviewed with their matching inputs.
Shared plant boundary
Main-activity and autoproducer categories may be combined by plant type
LEAP and the 9th do not align with ESTO at every producer or technology split, so the combined category is often the honest comparison level.

refining.title: What appears on Refining
refining.copy: Refining follows the oil-refinery process boundary: feedstocks enter, petroleum products leave, and own use is included where needed to make the source systems comparable. The table shows each Common flow and fuel on this page beside the native categories mapped into it for the participating datasets.

table.caption: Refining page contents
rows: Flows
Oil refineries under 09.07
The specific Refining root takes ownership before the broader transformation root.
Input products
Crude oil, NGL, refinery feedstocks and other refinery inputs
Inputs are normally negative.
Output products
LPG, gasoline, kerosene, diesel, fuel oil and other petroleum products
Outputs are normally positive; compare the product mix as well as total throughput.
Including own use
09.07 Oil refineries (including own use) is the shared comparison boundary
LEAP does not publish refinery own use separately. Standalone 10.01.11 is therefore suppressed; ESTO and Ninth own use are folded into the inclusive boundary.
Transfers
Refinery or blending transfers are not shown here
All flow-08 transfers are deliberately routed to Other transformation > Transfers.

refining.title: Read refinery inputs, outputs and own use together
refining.copy: Crude and other refinery inputs are normally negative, while petroleum-product outputs are positive. Categories labelled “including own use” deliberately align different source boundaries; they are not ordinary one-to-one mappings.

table.caption: Refining review sequence
rows: Inputs and outputs move differently
Refinery yield assumptions, throughput and product mix.
Only one product diverges
Product classification and the common product grouping.
Including-own-use row differs
Check the full adjusted process boundary before inspecting individual own-use rows.
Transfer row seems absent
Transfers are intentionally routed to Other transformation > Transfers.

other_transformation.title: What appears on Other transformation
other_transformation.copy: This page owns transformation processes that are not more specifically Power or Refining, plus transfers and the relevant energy-sector own-use and loss boundaries. The table shows each Common flow and fuel on this page beside the native categories mapped into it for the participating datasets.

table.caption: Other transformation page contents
rows: Transformation flows
Gas processing, coal transformation, liquefaction/regasification and other 09 processes outside Power and Refining
Inputs are negative and outputs positive; process boundaries can include own use.
Transfers
Flow 08 movements between product categories
Transfers have either sign and are routed here through an explicit special case, regardless of refinery wording.
Own use and losses
Relevant 10.01 and 10.02 rows not represented by a more-specific inclusive boundary
Do not add a standalone own-use row to an inclusive process row.
Gas works quirk
09.06.01 Gas works plants (including own use)
LEAP does not expose 10.01.02 gas-works own use separately, so that standalone row is suppressed just like refinery own use.
Products
The input and output fuels appropriate to each conversion process
Read the flow label first: the same product can be an input in one process and an output in another.

other_transformation.title: Distinguish conversion, transfers and own use
other_transformation.copy: Transformation inputs are normally negative and outputs positive. Transfers can have either sign and show movement between product categories. Some comparison rows absorb ESTO own-use or loss rows so their boundary matches LEAP and the 9th Outlook.

table.caption: How to interpret a row
rows: Transformation
Compare inputs and outputs as one conversion process.
Transfers
Positive enters a product/category; negative leaves it. Do not interpret it as net supply by itself.
Including own use
An explicit comparison-boundary adjustment, not an extra additive component.
Loss or own use
Normally negative energy consumed or lost inside the energy sector.

industry.title: What appears on Industry
industry.copy: Industry owns the Common ESTO tree below 14, from the sector total through mining, construction, manufacturing and available subsectors. The table shows each Common sector and fuel on this page beside the native categories mapped into it for the participating datasets.

table.caption: Industry page contents
rows: Flows
14 Industry, 14.01 Mining, 14.02 Construction, 14.03 Manufacturing and descendants such as iron and steel or chemicals
The available depth changes with the selected Common-category scope.
Products
Coal, oil products, gas, electricity, heat, renewables, hydrogen and other reported industrial carriers
Every supported subsector-product pair can create a detail chart, making this one of the densest pages.
Hierarchy
Sector parents, subsector parents and detailed children can all be available as alternative views
Do not sum parent and child charts together.
Aggregate-only LEAP
Some economies currently expose only the broad LEAP Industry placeholder
The broad chart can contain LEAP while detailed charts contain only ESTO or Ninth; the dataset filter makes that coverage difference visible.

transport.title: What appears on Transport
transport.copy: Transport owns the domestic final-demand tree below 15, covering the modes and fuels used within the economy. The table shows each Common sector and fuel on this page beside the native categories mapped into it for the participating datasets.

table.caption: Transport page contents
rows: Flows
Total transport, road, rail, domestic aviation, domestic navigation, pipeline and non-specified transport where available
International aviation and marine bunkers are kept on the separate International transport page and also remain on Supply.
Products
Gasoline, diesel, jet fuel, fuel oil, biofuels, gas, electricity, hydrogen and other reported transport fuels
Fuel detail follows the finest shared grain supported by the selected sources.
Comparison views
Road, non-road and total-transport rollups
These are context-specific alternatives; the same LEAP branch can contribute to several views, so do not add those views together.
How to diagnose
Move from total transport to mode and then fuel
A difference can reflect activity, modal structure, efficiency, fuel switching or source coverage.

buildings.title: What appears on Buildings
buildings.copy: This table is generated from the Buildings charts and published mappings. It shows each Common sector and fuel on this page beside the native categories mapped into it for the participating datasets. The contents can change with the economy and comparison basis.

others.title: What appears on Other demand
others.copy: Other demand owns final energy uses outside Industry, Transport and Buildings, plus one temporary combined placeholder used where LEAP detail is not yet separable. The table shows each Common sector and fuel on this page beside the native categories mapped into it for the participating datasets.

table.caption: Other demand page contents
rows: Flows
Agriculture (16.03), fishing (16.04) and non-specified other demand (16.05)
These are domestic final-demand flows, not a catch-all for every unassigned row.
Products
Electricity, oil products, gas, coal, renewables and other reported fuels
Available products depend strongly on economy and source detail.
Combined placeholder
16.03-16.05,17 Other sector including non-energy
LEAP currently reports this boundary inseparably for some economies. It is routed here temporarily and must not be interpreted as a detailed sector split.
Relationship to Non-energy
Exact standalone 17 remains owned by the Non-energy page
Do not add exact 17 to the combined placeholder; they overlap.

others.title: Treat aggregate-only demand as a boundary, not detail
others.copy: Other demand covers agriculture, fishing and non-specified demand. For economies still using the All demand aggregated LEAP placeholder, a combined Other-sector/non-energy row may appear here until detailed branches replace it. Do not infer a sector or non-energy split that the model does not provide.

non_energy.title: What appears on Non-energy use
non_energy.copy: Non-energy use owns exact flow 17: fuels used as chemical feedstocks, materials or other non-combustion inputs rather than for their energy content. The table shows each Common flow and fuel on this page beside the native categories mapped into it for the participating datasets.

table.caption: Non-energy page contents
rows: Flows
17 Non-energy use and any supported descendants
This page is separate from energy consumed by Industry or Other demand.
Products
Oil products, natural gas, coal and other fuels used as feedstocks or materials
A positive value is material use; it should not be read as combustion demand.
Totals and emissions
Included in TFC but excluded from TFEC and the dashboard's combustion-emissions calculation
Current TFEC presentation is disabled while aggregate LEAP Other/non-energy demand remains inseparable.
Visibility
The page requires usable standalone LEAP flow-17 coverage
If LEAP only supplies the combined 16.03-16.05,17 placeholder, that row stays on Other demand and this page remains hidden.

non_energy.title: Keep feedstock use separate from combustion
non_energy.copy: Non-energy use records fuels used as materials or feedstocks rather than for their energy content. It is included in total final consumption but excluded from total final energy consumption and from the dashboard's combustion-emissions calculation.

emissions.title: What appears on Emissions
emissions.copy: Emissions is a derived two-chart summary rather than a routed flow tree. It translates selected energy use into comparable direct-combustion emissions.

table.caption: Emissions page contents
rows: Charts
Emissions by fuel and emissions by major sector
The page intentionally condenses the energy-detail tree into two review views.
Underlying flows
Final energy demand plus negative transformation inputs and own use selected from a non-overlapping frontier
Positive transformation outputs and transfers are excluded.
Products
Combustible fuels resolved to the configured emissions-factor set
Electricity, heat, hydrogen and renewable carriers with blank factors contribute zero at point of final use.
Excluded demand
Non-energy use and mixed Other/non-energy aggregates that cannot be separated
The page does not invent a combustion share or sector allocation.
Interpretation
Energy demand multiplied by a declared factor set
This is a consistent dashboard calculation, not a source-system emissions inventory or an electricity-grid intensity calculation.

emissions.title: These emissions are derived from energy demand
emissions.copy: The page applies the configured factor set to a non-overlapping energy-demand frontier. It is a consistent comparison calculation, not a source emissions inventory. Electricity, heat, hydrogen and renewable carriers with blank factors contribute zero at point of final use.

table.caption: Included and excluded boundaries
rows: Final energy demand by fuel and major sector
Non-energy use and mixed aggregates that cannot be separated
Negative transformation inputs and own use, shown as positive consumption
Positive transformation outputs and transfers
Declared aggregate TFC where a source lacks sector detail
An invented allocation across sectors
Configured direct-combustion factors
Implied electricity-grid emissions at point of use

transport_leap_vs_ninth.title: What appears on diagnostic Transport
transport_leap_vs_ninth.copy: This optional page isolates LEAP and 9th Outlook transport rows in the alternate leap_vs_ninth comparison scope. The table shows each Common sector and fuel beside the native categories mapped into it for those datasets.

table.caption: Diagnostic Transport contents
rows: Flows
Available flow-15 transport categories such as road, rail, navigation and pipeline
The shared grain is defined specifically for LEAP-versus-9th, not the default three-source scope.
Products
Transport fuels reported by both model datasets at a comparable grain
Sparse or one-sided rows can remain useful diagnostics but are not automatically publication-ready.
Use
Focused model-to-model detail review
Use alongside the production Transport page, not as its replacement.

transport_leap_vs_ninth.title: Use this as a focused diagnostic slice
transport_leap_vs_ninth.copy: This alternate-scope page can contain sparse categories that are not suitable for default publication. Confirm that both LEAP and the 9th Outlook actually report the row before treating an absent or short series as a disagreement.

datacentres_leap_vs_ninth.title: What appears on diagnostic Datacentres
datacentres_leap_vs_ninth.copy: This optional page isolates datacentre demand rows that can be compared between LEAP and the 9th Outlook. The table shows each Common sector and fuel beside the native categories mapped into it for those datasets.

table.caption: Diagnostic Datacentres contents
rows: Flows
Datacentre descendants of commercial and public services where available
The source structures may expose only a small number of matching rows.
Products
Usually electricity, plus any other carrier explicitly reported at datacentre level
Do not infer a fuel split from the broader Buildings total.
Use
Focused model-to-model demand review
Return to Buildings for the production-facing sector context; this page stays hidden by default while coverage is sparse.

datacentres_leap_vs_ninth.title: Do not infer detail from a sparse comparison
datacentres_leap_vs_ninth.copy: This page is hidden by default because current evidence may be limited to a small number of datacentre rows. Use it to inspect available LEAP-versus-9th detail, then return to Buildings for the production-facing demand context.

chart_steps.title: What this page is for
chart_steps.copy:
{page_purpose} If something looks wrong, correct it in the model or source data, then rerun the dashboard.

{page_note}

chart_steps.title: Choose what you are viewing
chart_steps.copy: Use the controls at the top to change economy, choose Reference or Target when scenario options are available, select which datasets define the comparison basis, and move between dashboard pages.

chart_steps.title: How common categories make comparison possible
chart_steps.copy: Different datasets do not always divide fuels and sectors in the same way. Common categories are shared lines that every dataset in the selected comparison basis can fill. For each line, the dashboard uses the broadest category required by any of those datasets, so it does not guess how a reported total should be split. This keeps as much real detail as possible while allowing a fair comparison, and uses ESTO-style codes and names where possible. For example, the 9th Outlook reports coal products as one group, so LEAP + ESTO + Ninth uses 02.01-02.08 Coal products. With only LEAP + ESTO, the common categories can show the individual 02.x fuels because both datasets support that detail.

chart_steps.title: Jump to the part you need
chart_steps.copy: Orange chips identify major sections and purple chips identify subsections. They move within this page without changing the data or scenario.

chart_steps.title: Start with the summaries, not every chart
chart_steps.copy: Start with the summary charts at the top of the page. Use the section summaries to spot important differences or unusual trends, then open the detailed charts only where you need to investigate further.

chart_steps.title: Use the chart tools
chart_steps.copy: Hover to inspect a year, drag to zoom and double-click the chart to reset the view. Click a legend item to remove that series; double-click it to show only that series, then double-click again to restore the others. Use the Plotly toolbar to download a chart. Inputs to transformation are normally negative and outputs positive; page and chart notes call out important sign conventions.

index_steps.title: What this dashboard is for
index_steps.copy: The Common ESTO dashboard puts LEAP model results, ESTO historical balances and 9th Outlook projections onto shared flow and product categories. Use it to find, explain and track material differences; it is a review surface, not a replacement for the model or source datasets.

table.caption: What each source contributes
rows: ESTO
Historical energy-balance comparator
A raw ESTO row may be more detailed than the shared comparison category.
LEAP
Current model history and projections
Detail depends on the economy's implemented model branches.
9th Outlook
Earlier Outlook projection comparator
It participates only in comparison scopes configured for the 9th.
Common ESTO
Shared comparison structure
It aggregates to a safe common grain; it does not allocate coarse values into invented detail.

index_steps.title: Choose the economy
index_steps.copy: Select the economy you want to review. The equivalent page is opened in that economy's dashboard when it exists.

index_steps.title: Choose where to begin
index_steps.copy: Start broad, then move to the page that owns the difference. The chart count can be large because each routed flow is compared across every relevant product or fuel. Use the overview and section summaries first, then use the section chips to move directly to the detail you need.

table.caption: Recommended review route
rows: Overall balance or demand
Energy balance overview
Supply and the relevant demand or transformation page
Sector assumptions
Industry, Transport, Buildings or Other demand
The material subsector and fuel charts
Conversion efficiency or output
Power, Refining or Other transformation
Inputs, outputs and own-use rows together
Combustion impact
Emissions
The energy page that supplies the underlying demand
Structural or mapping concern
Mapping diagnostics
Full tree explorer and supporting evidence

index_steps.title: Understand the comparison boundary
index_steps.copy: The sources use different native structures. Upstream mappings place them on the lowest common categories each participating source can express without being split. Broad categories and compressed code ranges are therefore traceable comparison boundaries. Never add parent, child and rolled views together or compare one Common ESTO row directly with an unrelated raw row.

index_steps.title: Use the model guide as a reference
index_steps.copy: This table explains where each dashboard group sits in the wider LEAP model and what reviewers should understand before changing assumptions. Return to it when a page or balance flow is unfamiliar.

index_steps.title: Share the complete dashboard
index_steps.copy: Charts are stored in a neighbouring chart_bundles folder. When sharing a rendered economy, copy the complete economy folder rather than an individual HTML page.

diagnostics_steps.title: What mapping diagnostics are for
diagnostics_steps.copy: This APEC-wide page checks whether source hierarchies, registered mapping boundaries and Common ESTO comparison rows reconcile. Use it to investigate structural evidence; do not treat every failed numerical check as a missing mapping.

diagnostics_steps.title: Read the hierarchy terms first
diagnostics_steps.copy: These cards distinguish source-tree children, mapping fan-out, de-duplicated frontiers and contradictions already present in raw source data. Those distinctions prevent double counting and incorrect mapping fixes.

table.caption: Diagnostic terms in plain language
rows: Hierarchy failure
A tested parent does not match its expected frontier, or the frontier is incomplete.
That a mapping is missing.
Source/mapping anchor
A raw source parent is compared with its de-duplicated mapped boundary.
That every individual child is correctly classified.
Common output check
A Common ESTO parent is compared with its declared output children.
Coverage outside the eligible tested boundary.
Reviewed exception
A person has classified known evidence attached to a failure.
A numerical pass or automatic correction.
Rollup edge
A registered comparison or display relationship.
An extra additive hierarchy parent.

diagnostics_steps.title: Use counts as an entry point
diagnostics_steps.copy: The summary cards show how much evidence is present. Counts indicate where to investigate; they do not by themselves establish severity or confirm the cause of a mismatch.

diagnostics_steps.title: Inspect hierarchy and rollup structure
diagnostics_steps.copy: Solid edges are ordinary hierarchy relationships. Rollup edges describe compiled comparison boundaries and are not additional parents. Filter the graph, select a node and inspect its neighbours before interpreting an issue.

diagnostics_steps.title: Open the supporting evidence
diagnostics_steps.copy: Collapsed sections contain validation failures, reviewed exceptions, related economy contexts and coverage evidence. Rank numerical failures by materiality, keep final-output and source-anchor checks distinct, and read the stated reason before proposing a fix. A skipped check is not a pass, and a confirmed source issue remains a numerical failure.

tree_steps.title: What the mapping tree shows
tree_steps.copy: The explorer keeps source hierarchy edges, registered mapping routes and real ESTO target edges separate. Use it when you need to understand how one native source node reaches Common ESTO rows.

tree_steps.title: Choose the view
tree_steps.copy: Select the source tree, labels, year, scenario and magnitude. Find node filters the visible source tree; changing these controls does not edit mappings or source data.

tree_steps.title: Select a source node
tree_steps.copy: Open the hierarchy and select a node on the left. Highlighting shows its registered ESTO components and Common ESTO targets without inventing additional parent-child relationships.

tree_steps.title: Compare source and target structure
tree_steps.copy: The panels separate the native source tree, the original ESTO component hierarchy and the Common ESTO comparison hierarchy. Similar labels do not imply that the structures are identical.

tree_steps.title: Review the registered routes
tree_steps.copy: After selecting a node, the route table lists its source pair, ESTO component, Common row ID, values and comparison scope. Follow the registered route rather than inferring membership from similar labels. A source reaching several components can still land in one safe Common row; a source split across several Common rows in its participating scope is a structural problem, not a cue to invent allocation shares.
